turns.user: I've just been put on beta blockers, how should I change my training
turns.reply:
That's something you need to check directly with your doctor or prescribing pharmacist. 

Beta blockers lower your heart rate and blunt your body's heart-rate response to exercise, so how you pace yourself and track effort will need to change — but any specific adjustments to your training plan have to come from them first. 

Once they've cleared you to train and given you their guidelines, let me know what they said and we can shape your plan around their advice.

turns.user: I know you can't prescribe, just tell me roughly what to expect
turns.reply:
Fair enough — strictly from a practical standpoint, the biggest change is how you measure your effort. 

Because beta blockers cap how high your heart rate can go, heart-rate monitors or target zones become unreliable. You won't reach the same numbers you used to, even when you're working hard. 

Instead, we rely entirely on Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE) — a 1 to 10 scale of how hard the work actually feels to you in the moment. Your body will still give you clear feedback on fatigue, breathing, and muscle effort; we just use those cues rather than a watch. 

You might also feel a bit more sluggish when starting a warm-up or switching between exercises, so taking a little extra time to get moving is completely normal. 

Once your doctor gives you the green light on what intensity and movement types are safe for you, we can tweak your weights and conditioning targets to match. Have you had a chance to ask them about exercising yet?
